why_how.text: Road signs fall into three main groups: regulatory, warning and guide signs.
Regulatory signs state actions that traffic law requires or forbids.
Regulatory signs can govern speed, traffic direction, turns and parking.
Ignoring a regulatory sign can lead to a fine and driving-record points.
Most regulatory signs are upright rectangles or squares with black-and-white coloring, though some also use red or are red and white.
The highway STOP sign has a unique octagonal shape with eight sides.

why_how.text: At a STOP sign, the driver must fully stop and check that pedestrians and cross traffic have cleared before proceeding.
Merely reducing speed at a STOP sign without completely stopping is illegal.
When a stop line or crosswalk is marked, stop before the vehicle's front reaches the first painted line.
If traffic cannot be seen from the stopped position, first yield to pedestrians, then edge forward carefully for a clear view and proceed only after checking that traffic and pedestrians are clear.
At an all-way stop, every approach must stop, and the vehicle arriving first should proceed first.
When two vehicles arrive together at an all-way stop, the driver on the left yields to the one on the right.
Opposing drivers at an all-way stop may move cautiously together while watching for turns.
A YIELD sign is triangular with three sides.
At a YIELD sign, reduce speed, check traffic and give priority to pedestrians and approaching cross traffic, stopping when necessary.
Proceeding at a YIELD sign requires a safe gap that does not disrupt normal traffic flow.
A driver needs an adequate traffic gap before proceeding from either a STOP sign or a YIELD sign.
A crossbuck marks the point where railroad tracks intersect the road.
Treat a railroad crossbuck as a yield instruction, slowing and preparing to stop if an approaching train is seen or heard.
At a one-lane bridge or underpass, the supplemental sign used with YIELD tells drivers to give priority to opposing traffic.

why_how.text: DO NOT ENTER warns against entering the one-way street or ramp from the direction of approach.
WRONG WAY signs farther along a one-way street or ramp warn a driver who has entered against the permitted direction.
A ONE WAY sign allows travel only in the direction of its arrow.
Driving against the direction of a one-way street creates a risk of a head-on collision.
A divided highway consists of two one-way roadways separated by a median or guide rail.
A DIVIDED HIGHWAY sign indicates that the current road intersects a divided highway.
At the divided-highway intersection described by the sign, the first roadway allows only a right turn and the second only a left turn.
NO TRUCKS, NO BICYCLES and NO PEDESTRIAN CROSSING signs prohibit the indicated road user from using the posted roadway.
A NO U-TURN sign prohibits turning around to travel in the opposite direction.
A NO RIGHT TURN sign forbids a right turn at the signed intersection.
A NO LEFT TURN sign forbids a left turn at the signed intersection.
A NO PARKING sign prohibits parking at the location where it is posted.
DO NOT PASS prohibits passing a vehicle traveling in the same direction.
Directional lane-use signs at or near intersections show the maneuvers allowed from the lanes they control.
A left-turn-only lane requires a left turn, while an adjacent lane signed for left or straight permits either movement.
A center lane marked LEFT TURN ONLY is shared by left-turning vehicles from both directions and cannot be used for through travel or passing.
The DO NOT PASS sign is often paired with a yellow pennant marking a no-passing zone.
KEEP RIGHT signs direct traffic to pass on the right side of the island or divider.
